claims.text: The target material is a high-melting refractory material.
The initial simulation cell contains coexisting solid and liquid regions near the melting temperature.
The two-phase coexistence method is implemented by initializing coexisting solid and liquid phases.
Efficient sampling methods can capture solid-liquid phase equilibrium.
Machine-learning interatomic potentials are an example of an efficient sampling technique for this calculation.
The calculation is performed at high temperatures where solid and liquid phases coexist.
Constant-volume, constant-pressure, or constant-energy conditions can be selected as appropriate for simulating phase equilibrium.
The solid-liquid interface mediates the energy and structural balance that defines the melting point.
The two-phase coexistence method directly simulates solid-liquid phase equilibrium.
The two-phase coexistence method can determine the melting temperature without thermodynamic integration over multiple states.
The method can determine entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
The method yields melting properties with accuracy comparable to full ab initio free-energy calculations.
The method has significantly lower computational cost than full ab initio free-energy calculations.
The reduced computational cost makes the method suitable for high-throughput screening of refractory materials.
Traditional ab initio free-energy calculations use density functional theory, thermodynamic integration, and ab initio molecular-dynamics trajectories.
The reliability of the approach depends on the construction and transferability of the efficient sampling model.
Very sharp solid-liquid interfaces or extreme melting conditions may limit the method's accuracy.
Machine-learning potentials may not reproduce full-DFT accuracy across all refractory materials, particularly complex alloys.
